catalog_quote: Stress is typically on the penultimate syllable, regardless of the number of syllables in the root, as could be seen in (2)–(4) above. Examples of roots with stress on the last syllable are e.g. aˈbi ‘sour’, maŋˈgo ‘banana’, bibiˈtoŋ ‘butterfly’ and amˈgor ‘shout’. See also minˈlen ‘woman’, pinˈca ‘side’ and taraˈmus ‘fairytale’, introduced in (2) and (3). Some of the words with root-final stress appear to be loans from Kalamang. This neighbouring Papuan language has unpredictable stress but has a slight preference for the right edge (Visser, 2022, 74). Examples are taˈpar ‘k.o. kangaroo’ and saˈnoŋ ‘thatched roof’, which have the same meaning and stress pattern in Kalamang. There are also words that are the same in Uruangnirin and Kalamang except for the stress: lusi ‘eagle’ is an example. In Uruangnirin, it is pronounced ˈlusi, in Kalamang luˈsi. new_statements.rule_in_words: Default word stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the root whatever its length (ˈsi.ka, ku.ˈte.na, ma.ka.ˈni.ni, ka.na.ˈba.raf); a lexically listed minority of roots carry final stress (aˈbi, maŋˈgo, bibiˈtoŋ, amˈgor, minˈlen, pinˈca, taraˈmus, kaˈsuk), several of them loans from Kalamang (taˈpar, saˈnoŋ), and the authors attribute the final-stress set to Kalamang contact. No weight conditioning is proposed; no antepenultimate or other patterns reported.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said about secondary stress in any of the three sources.
new_statements.exceptions: Final-stress roots: aˈbi 'sour', maŋˈgo 'banana', bibiˈtoŋ 'butterfly', amˈgor 'shout', minˈlen 'woman', pinˈca 'side', taraˈmus 'fairytale', kaˈsuk 'man' (Visser 2026), taˈpar 'k.o. kangaroo', saˈnoŋ 'thatched roof' (Kalamang loans with Kalamang stress); contrast ˈlusi 'eagle' (Uruangnirin) vs luˈsi (Kalamang). Visser 2026 OTC p. 20 calls the final-stress exceptions 'many'. Visser 2026 sketch notes final-stressed minlen/kasuk reduplicate their final syllable (minlenlen, kasuksuk).
new_statements.domain_note: Stated over roots/citation forms ('regardless of the number of syllables in the root'); transcriptions are of isolated lexemes from a recorded wordlist (IPA with stress marks in the 1,400-item appendix). Nothing explicit on whether subject-index prefixes or reduplication shift stress; prefixes are pre-root so penult-of-root and penult-of-word coincide for suffixless forms. Phrase-level prosody deferred to Gunnarsson 2025 (phonological word / accentual phrase / intonational phrase).
new_statements.identity_note: All three Visser sources describe the Faur-Kiaba dialect (fieldwork in Kiaba village, 2022-2025); Visser 2026 OTC notes minimal dialect differences vs Tarak-Tuberwasak (lexical items, /ŋg/ > /g/ simplification), nothing said about dialectal stress differences. Language also called Rwangnirin / Wangnirin / Karas Darat. Glottolog urua1244 has no dialect subdivisions.

sources.note: Sec. 2.5 'Stress assignment' p. xxxii: stress typically penultimate regardless of root length; a set of lexical exceptions with final stress (aˈbi, maŋˈgo, bibiˈtoŋ, amˈgor, minˈlen, pinˈca, taraˈmus), some of them Kalamang loans; sec. 4 p. xxxvi repeats 'typically on the penultimate syllable.. a fair number of examples with stress on the final syllable'. Also notes /e/ realisation interacts with stress position (sec. 2.2). Wordlist appendix carries IPA with stress marks.

sources.note: Sec. 2 'Phonology' p. clviii: 'Stress is typically on the penult (ˈfodan 'tikal leaf'), with some exceptions where stress is on the last syllable (kaˈsuk 'man'). Some of the words with final stress are loans from Kalamang (saˈnoŋ 'thatched roof').' Cites Gunnarsson 2025 for intonation (phonological word, accentual phrase, intonational phrase). Sec. on reduplication (p. clxii area): final-stressed minlen, kasuk reduplicate the LAST syllable (minlenlen, kasuksuk), attributed to their final stress.
